summary:
During long-duration space missions, astronauts face serious health risks from microgravity, cosmic radiation, isolation and disrupted sleep. Most of their health monitoring is their own responsibility, and small changes can easily go unnoticed under a demanding mission schedule. On Moon and Mars missions, communication delays also make immediate medical support impossible.
Today, health monitoring on the International Space Station relies largely on periodic medical checks and on assessments by flight surgeons on the ground. Radiation dose is usually tracked with separate devices. This approach works in low Earth orbit, where communication is almost instant, but it falls short on deep-space missions.
ASTROVITAL is web-based software designed to continuously monitor astronaut health. It brings physiological data and radiation dose together in a single two-part dashboard. Alerts are based on each astronaut’s own normal values, so the monitoring is personalized. The recommendation system does more than flag a risk: it explains step by step what should be done and why. The system is tested on realistic mission scenarios and real NASA and NOAA data [NASA OSDR OSD-575 (Inspiration4 blood serum data), NASA DONKI (space weather event catalog) and NOAA GOES proton flux data]. As a result, astronauts can make reliable decisions without waiting for Earth, late diagnoses can be avoided and the crew’s workload is reduced.
details:
ASTROVITAL - Detailed Report

ASTROVITAL is web-based software designed to continuously monitor the health of astronauts on long-duration space missions. It collects health data such as heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), body temperature and radiation dose in a single two-part dashboard and displays them in real-time charts. It builds a personal health profile for each astronaut and compares new measurements both with generally accepted values and with that person's own normal values. When a value crosses a limit or an unusual trend begins, it gives an early warning through a color-coded system. The main screen features a rotating 3D human model. Vital signs appear as colored points on the corresponding parts of the body. Clicking a point shows the analysis of that vital sign and how consistent it is with the others. Astronauts can select the symptoms they feel (such as headache, chills or shortness of breath), and the system includes them in its assessment. The recommendation system explains to the crew step by step what to do, and every recommendation comes with a “why this recommendation?” explanation. The crew can send health reports to the flight surgeon on Earth. Reports wait in a queue and are delivered with a realistic communication delay.

ASTROVITAL is built on real data and accepted standards. We chose which health risks to monitor based on the five hazards of human spaceflight defined by NASA's Human Research Program. Alert thresholds are based on the NEWS2 clinical score used in hospitals and on each astronaut's own baseline values. Radiation dose limits are taken from the NASA-STD-3001 standard. Dose rates in the mission profiles are based on measurements by NASA's Curiosity rover during its cruise to Mars and by Chang'e-4 on the lunar surface. Live radiation data comes from NOAA's GOES satellites. The solar storm of 10 September 2017 can also be replayed using real GOES-13 data and NASA DONKI records. We tested our personal baseline method on real blood data collected by NASA from the Inspiration4 crew (OSD-575). Of 60 post-flight measurements, standard lab ranges flagged only 4, while the personal baseline caught 17; 13 of these looked “normal” by lab ranges. Using NASA data takes ASTROVITAL beyond a concept study and turns it into a prototype that can be adapted to real space missions.

During long-duration space missions, astronauts can face serious health risks from microgravity, cosmic radiation, isolation and disrupted sleep. Despite these risks, most of the work of tracking health data is the astronauts' own responsibility. Under a demanding mission schedule, some changes in the body can go unnoticed and illnesses can be diagnosed late. Another factor that makes the problem worse is dependence on Earth. On Moon and Mars missions, communication delays make it impossible to get immediate medical support from the ground team. An answer to an astronaut's question can take minutes, and in that time a small problem can turn into a serious danger. In short, astronauts need a reliable system that monitors their health, spots risks early and tells them what to do without waiting for Earth. ASTROVITAL was developed to fill exactly this gap.

ASTROVITAL can help prevent late diagnosis of illnesses and delays in treatment. Because unusual changes are noticed before symptoms get worse, problems can be brought under control before they grow. By taking over health monitoring, the system reduces the crew's workload, so astronauts can spend their time on science and mission operations. Thanks to the recommendation system, they can make fast and reliable decisions without waiting for a reply from Earth. Reducing dependence on Earth for health monitoring is critical, especially for Moon and Mars missions. Knowing that their health is being monitored continuously also gives astronauts confidence. The data collected during missions can also help plan future space missions more safely.

What makes ASTROVITAL creative is its holistic view of health. By combining physiological data and radiation exposure in the same dashboard, it shows the astronaut's overall condition at a glance. Alerts are not based on the same limits for everyone but on each astronaut's own normal values, which makes the monitoring personalized. The system does not just display data; it also says what should be done. In this way, it goes beyond a monitoring screen and becomes a decision support tool for the crew.

Our team considered several key factors when designing the system. Because of communication delays, our top priority was for the system to work independently of Earth. Taking the astronauts' busy schedule into account, we designed the interface to be simple and to require little interaction. The color-coded system makes the situation clear at a glance. Unnecessary alerts tire astronauts and reduce their trust in the system, so we aimed to reduce false alarms by comparing values with personal baselines. Because health data is sensitive, no data is sent to an external server; all calculations are done on the device itself. Finally, we built the system with an extensible structure so that new sensors can be added in the future and it can be adapted to longer missions.

 

The app works fully offline and needs no server or installation, so it can run on any tablet or laptop on board. It could also be useful on Earth: at remote stations, on polar expeditions and in telemedicine.

 

Tools, languages, hardware and software informations:

 

Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (no framework, no build step)

Libraries: Three.js (3D human model), Chart.js (charts)

3D model: MakeHuman (CC0 license), prepared with a Python script

Fonts: IBM Plex Sans / Mono (Open Font License)

Data:

NASA OSDR OSD-575

NOAA SWPC GOES real-time data feeds

NOAA NCEI GOES-13 archive

NASA DONKI

Standards: NEWS2 (Royal College of Physicians), NASA-STD-3001, NOAA Space Weather Scales

Offline support: Service Worker and localStorage

Hosting: GitHub and GitHub Pages

Hardware: Standard laptop and web browser only; no special hardware

AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding and writing assistant. All design decisions, the recommendation rules and the testing were done by our team.
